cards.explanation: The answer is True. The first woman says, “We were alone, with no one in the house but the two of us.” By her account, it's just the two women in that house. It's her word against the other woman's word. Keep that in mind, friends, because it's what makes this case so tricky.

The answer is that the other woman swapped her dead son for the living one. That's what the first woman claims. She says the other woman got up in the middle of the night, took her son from her side while she slept, and put her own dead son in his place. Notice whose side this is: the other woman hasn't had her say yet. I think a swap in the dark is something you'd only catch in the morning light, but that's my guess.

The answer is False. There's no confession here. The first woman says she got up in the morning to nurse her son and found him dead. When she examined him, she realized he was not the son she had borne. She figured it out by looking at him, not because anyone admitted a thing.

The answer is living. The other woman says the living baby is hers: “the living one is my son and the dead one is your son.” That's the exact opposite of what the first woman said. The first woman insists right back, “No, the dead one is yours and the living one is mine.” Two women, one baby, and zero budging.

The answer is a sword. Solomon, Israel's king, says, “Bring me a sword.” Then they bring him one (1 Kings 3:24). It's a shocking thing to ask for in that moment. If it were me, I'd have asked for a long sit-down and a cookie, so there's a reason he's the king and I'm a stamper.

The answer is True. Solomon says, “Cut the living child in two and give half to one and half to the other.” It's a hard thing to hear, and I think the whole room felt it. Keep listening, friends, because the story isn't done with what this order does.

The answer is that she begs the king to give the baby to the other woman. She says, “Please, my lord, give her the living baby. Do not kill him!” She'd rather lose him than see him hurt. The text says she spoke because she yearned with compassion for her son.

The answer is compassion. The text says she “…yearned with compassion for her son.” That word explains why she says, “give her the living baby. Do not kill him!” Her plea is all about him staying alive. That's a mother's love in plain view.

The answer is that she says neither of them gets him, so cut him. Her words are, “He will be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!” Set that beside the other woman's plea, “Do not kill him!” Two women hear the same sword and give two completely different answers. I think that contrast is the whole moment.

The answer is the woman who begged to spare him. Solomon says, “Give the living baby to the first woman. By no means should you kill him; she is his mother.” She's the one who said, “Do not kill him!” The king's whole ruling points at her. His ruling gives the baby to the woman who begged for his life.

The answer is False. In his ruling, Solomon says, “By no means should you kill him; she is his mother.” He rules that the baby be given to the woman who begged for his life. The sword order came first, and then the ruling said the opposite.

The answer is False. They don't think he's too harsh. The text says, “When all Israel heard of the judgment the king had given, they stood in awe of him…” Awe is the reaction the text gives them. It doesn't give any complaint.

The answer is wisdom. The text says they saw that “…the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice.” It's the people's own conclusion about Solomon. They didn't just see a clever king. They saw wisdom from God at work in how he judged.
